text: And now a mistake: keeping the message in a plain variable. If you're new to React, you might keep the text in a plain variable the way plain JavaScript does. Same file, ContactForm.jsx, but watch line two. There's no useState anymore. Instead, it says let message equal an empty string. And inside the handler on line five, message equals e.target.value. The note marks it wrong. It changes a plain variable, so React never renders again. Everything else is just as before: the heading, the text area with its onChange, and the count, message.length out of two hundred. The user types hi. The box shows hi, but the count stays at zero. Take a look at figure ten, the contact form with a plain variable after the user types hi. The word hi is right there in the message box. And underneath, the count still reads zero out of two hundred. So why does the box show hi while the count stays at zero? Here is what happens on each key. The browser puts the letter into the box. The box has no value yet, so the browser keeps the letter there on its own. React calls handleMessageChange, and the handler changes the plain variable. But changing a plain variable does not ask React to render again, so React never calls ContactForm again. The count on the page is still the one React drew when the page opened, and it says zero. And there's a second problem. Even if something else made React render again, the first line of the component would run again. It would set message right back to an empty string. The fix is the state from lesson twelve. The setter keeps the text between renders and asks React to render again. Back in ContactForm.jsx, the top of the file is fixed. useState is imported again, and line four brings back message and set message starting empty. And line seven inside the handler is set message with e.target.value. It saves the text and asks React to render again. Now the count follows every letter, just like we saw before. One more thing. Inside the handler, message is still one letter behind. There is one more trap here. Suppose we add a log line to the handler just for a moment. It's only the handler this time, lines six to nine. The new line seven is console.log of message, and the note says it shows the text from before this key. Then line eight is our usual set message with e.target.value. The box holds were, W-H-E-R, and the user types E. The console shows were, not where. Why the old text? In lesson fifteen, you saw that each render sees its own fixed state values. The handler belongs to a render too. Here is the order. When the box held were, React rendered ContactForm. In that render, message is were, and the handler is made in that same render. The user types E, and the browser puts it into the box. React calls the handler from that render. Inside it, message is still were. Set message saves where, but only the next render will see it. So inside the handler, the new text lives only in e.target.value. That's why the handler saves e.target.value and never builds the new text from message. And now we take the log line out again before we go on. So principle one: onChange, React calls it on every key. When the page must react to what the user types, give the box onChange and save e.target.value with the setter. The count must move while the user types, so the text must reach state on every key. React's onChange is not the browser's change event, which waits for the user to leave the box. It fires on every key, like the browser's input event. By the time it runs, the browser has already put the new letter into the box. So e.target.value holds the whole new text. A plain variable cannot do this job because changing it never makes React render again. The right way looks like this: const message and set message from useState with an empty string and a text area tag whose onChange is an arrow calling set message with e.target.value. That saves the whole text on every key. The wrong way is let message equal an empty string and an onChange arrow that just assigns e.target.value to message. A plain variable like that never makes React render again.
